blocks.text: Revisions to the paper titled Domain-decomposed antiderivative transformation iterative method: A deep learning approach for weakly and Cauchy types singular integral equations
Manuscript Number: ELSCAM-D-26-01599
Dear Editor and Reviewers,

Thank you very much for your comments concerning our manuscript entitled "Domain-decomposed antiderivative transformation iterative method: A deep learning approach for weakly and Cauchy types singular integral equations". All of the comments have been taken into account, and the manuscript has been revised accordingly (revised portions in the revised manuscript have been marked in red color for easier identification purposes). Below is our description of the revision based on the reviewers' comments.
With kindest regards,
Yours Sincerely,
Dong Liu
Response to Reviewer #1:
1. Page 3, line no. 11 from top, for hyper-singular integral equations, “α≥2” seems to be “α > 1”. Otherwise, discuss the missing case 1 < α < 2.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We agree with the reviewer and have corrected the condition for hypersingular integral equations to “α > 1”.
The corresponding change appears on page 4 (line 102).
2. Page 4, line no. 16 from top, the statement “ and  are both continuous, the integrand  is also a continuous function.” seems to be wrong. For example, if  and , how  will be a continuous function.

blocks.text: 4. Motivation is not sufficiently stated in the introduction part. It should be clarified what advantages of the proposed technique are.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We have added the following explanation to the manuscript:

“Unlike traditional methods, the deep-learning approach proposed in this work builds the solution scheme directly from the original equation, without any model simplification. The solution process is well-organized and relatively simple to implement. Moreover, deep-learning approaches are widely regarded as a promising method for solving high-dimensional integro-differential equations. The proposed method may therefore provide a useful and potentially high-performance route for solving singular integral equations arising in fracture mechanics and other complex engineering problems.”
The corresponding change appears on page 2 (lines 66–72).

>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We have set the line spacing throughout the manuscript to 1.5 lines.

Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We have replaced R with ℝ in Eq. (9). The corresponding change appears on page 5 (line 156).
8. The authors should state in the paper what kind of the software package has used to obtain the required results in the beginning of the numerical examples section.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. At the beginning of the numerical-validation section (Section 6), we have added details of the software used to generate the reported results, as follows:

11. Moreover, there are some minor grammatical inconsistencies throughout the manuscript which need to be corrected.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We have carefully proofread and revised the grammar and language throughout the manuscript. Some representative examples of the revisions are given below:
"thus establishes new technical approaches" has been revised to "thus establishing new technical approaches" (see page 1, line 23).
"differential equations systems" has been revised to "differential equation systems" (see page 2, line 63).
All other grammatical and linguistic revisions have been marked in red in the revised manuscript.
Response to Reviewer #2:
1. Lack of theoretical analysis. The manuscript does not provide rigorous results regarding:
• Equivalence between the original singular integral equation and the transformed differential system;
• Stability of the proposed transformation;
• Convergence of the iterative neural-network procedure;
• Influence of the parameter ε introduced near singular points.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments.
Regarding the equivalence and stability of the transformation from the original singular integral equation to the differential system, we have added the following statement:

“By the Newton–Leibniz formula, if the kernel in an integral term is continuous over the solution domain, then, provided that a definite solution exists, the integral term and its antiderivative are in one-to-one correspondence. This establishes the equivalence between the original singular integral equation and the transformed differential system [1,28]. Because the antiderivative transformation of an integral term with a continuous kernel is mathematically rigorous, the transformation is stable.”
See Refs. [1,28] and the derivation in the main text, page 4, lines 127–131, Eqs. (9)–(11).

The convergence of neural-network iterative solvers for differential equations is a central research topic in scientific machine learning, and current studies in this field verify convergence mainly through numerical experiments. We have therefore added the following statement in Section 6.2:

“The experimental results show that the total loss of the proposed method decreases progressively with the iterations and then levels off, indicating that the computational process exhibits good convergence, as shown in Fig. 6.” See page 14, lines 320–322.

“Eleven values of 𝜀 were selected across different orders of magnitude, and five independent repeated runs were carried out for each value. The results show that for ε > 0.001 the prediction error decreases as ε decreases, whereas for ε < 0.001 the prediction error remains essentially unchanged.” See page 13, lines 312–314, and page 14, lines 318–320.

Response:

>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. Because D-AIM is a deep-learning method, we chose to compare it with the conventional PINN method. We have added the corresponding comparison to Section 6.2, with the main results summarized as follows:

“Fig. 8 shows the evolution of the total loss with the number of training epochs for the PINN method, and Fig. 9 compares the D-AIM solution, the PINN solution, and the analytical solution. The results show that the loss of the PINN method oscillates drastically during training and does not decrease to a converged level, resulting in a large error; the D-AIM method therefore exhibits a clear performance advantage over the conventional PINN in this example.”

3. Sensitivity to hyperparameters. The network architecture, loss weights, sampling strategy, and values of ε appear to be selected empirically. A sensitivity study would significantly strengthen the manuscript.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments.
We have carried out a systematic sensitivity analysis of ε in Section 6.2 and added the following statement:

“Eleven values of 𝜀 were selected across different orders of magnitude, and five independent repeated runs were carried out for each value. Fig. 7 shows the variation of the MSE with 𝜀, together with the error bars obtained from the repeated runs. The results show that for ε > 0.001 the prediction error decreases as ε decreases, whereas for ε < 0.001 the prediction error remains essentially unchanged.” See page 13, lines 312–314, and page 14, lines 318–320.

With reference to existing research on deep learning based PDE solvers, hyperparameters such as the network architecture, sampling strategy, and loss weights still lack a well-established theoretical foundation, and are mainly determined empirically and through experiments. We therefore followed established PINN practice and selected the hyperparameters in our numerical experiments. A theoretical study of hyperparameter selection will be pursued in future work. We added the following sentence to the outlook in Section 7:

“Future research will focus on theoretically analyzing the convergence and stability of the multi-network iterative deep learning method and quantitatively evaluating its time and space complexity. Further theoretical studies will also examine how key hyperparameters, including network architecture, loss weights, and sampling strategies, affect solver performance.”
The corresponding changes appear on page 18-19 (lines 390–393).

4. Computational efficiency. Training time, hardware specifications, convergence history, and computational complexity are not discussed. These aspects are important when assessing the practical usefulness of deep learning-based numerical methods.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments.
We have added the following description of the hardware configuration to Section 6:

“In this section, all numerical examples were trained on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti GPU. The networks were implemented, differentiated automatically and trained using PyTorch 2.12.0 with CUDA 12.6 acceleration, and the complete workflow was run in Python 3.13.”
The corresponding change appears on page 10 (lines 273–275).
We also added a discussion of training time and convergence history to Section 6.2, as follows:

“In the above computing environment, each training run took approximately 5400 s on average. Fig. 6 shows the evolution of the total loss with the number of training epochs. The loss decreases steadily and levels off at roughly 500,000 epochs, indicating that training has converged.” The corresponding change appears on pages 13-14 (lines 314–317).

Regarding computational complexity, since the quantitative analysis of the complexity of deep learning is a recognized challenge in the field, we will pursue this issue in our future research. We have added the following clarification to the outlook section:
“Future research will focus on theoretically analyzing the convergence and stability of the multi-network iterative deep learning method and quantitatively evaluating its time and space complexity.”
The corresponding change appears on page 18 (lines 390–391).
5. The literature review should better position the proposed method with respect to PINNs, XPINNs, BINNs, DeepONets, and neural operator frameworks.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We have expanded the literature review in Section 1 to clarify how the proposed method relates to these five classes of methods, as follows:

“In recent years, deep learning has been used not only for differential equations [19-23] but also increasingly for integral equations. PINN-based methods have been developed for multidimensional Fredholm integral equations [24,25], volume integral equations [26], boundary integral equations [27] and other multidimensional integral equations with continuous kernels [28]. For integral equations with discontinuous coefficients, domain-decomposed XPINNs are often used to accommodate non-smooth solutions across interfaces [29]. DeepONet and neural-operator methods are suitable for solving a class of parameterized problems [21,30-32], thereby enhancing the generalization capability of deep learning based numerical computation. Most of these studies concern non-singular integral equations and evaluate the integral terms by numerical integration, which introduces additional discretization error. The boundary integral neural network (BINN) is an important exception: it converts a PDE into a boundary integral equation using a Green’s function and evaluates weakly singular and Cauchy-type singular integrals by regularization techniques. Its applicability, however, depends on the existence of the BIE formulation and the fundamental solution. In many non-linear problems, the unknowns in the interior region cannot be completely eliminated. Moreover, the fundamental solution may be hard to obtain or even not exist [27]. Therefore, it is necessary to explore new deep learning methods for solving singular integral equations.”
The corresponding change appears on page 2 (lines 42–57).
6. Several grammatical and stylistic issues remain and careful proofreading is recommended.
Response:
>> We thank the reviewer for these comments. We have carefully proofread and revised the grammar and language throughout the manuscript. Some representative examples of the revisions are given below:
"thus establishes new technical approaches" has been revised to "thus establishing new technical approaches" (see page 1, line 23).
"differential equations systems" has been revised to "differential equation systems" (see page 2, line 63).
All other grammatical and linguistic revisions have been marked in red in the revised manuscript.
